def: A *simple-declaration* or condition with a *structured-binding-declaration*, such as `auto [a, b] = e;`. The specifiers can only be `constexpr`, `constinit`, `static`, `thread_local`, `auto`, and cv-qualifiers, and it contains at most one pack.
A declaration whose specifier sequence contains `typedef`; each *declarator-id* in it is declared to be a typedef-name ([[dcl.typedef]]).
A declaration that is not a typedef declaration and in which the type associated with the *declarator-id* is a function type. The classification is made declarator by declarator.

A declaration that is not a typedef declaration and in which the type associated with the *declarator-id* is an object type or a **reference type**. If the type is neither a function nor an object/reference (e.g. `void`), the program is ill-formed.

The condition of a `static_assert`, contextually converted to `bool`, is `false`, and it is not in the context of a template definition; the program is then ill-formed. Since C++26 the message can be a computed string.
A name declared by `typedef` or an *alias-declaration* (`using X = T;`), i.e. a *typedef-name*; it **does not introduce a new type**, and its underlying entity is the aliased type.

An unnamed class or unnamed enumeration defined in a typedef declaration takes the first typedef-name for that type in the declaration as its name for linkage purposes, such as `S` in `typedef struct { int x; } S;`. Since C++20 such an unnamed class must be "C-compatible" (no member functions, base classes, default member initializers, or lambdas).

A function declared with `constexpr` or `consteval` (so immediate functions are also constexpr functions). It is implicitly inline and can appear in constant expressions; otherwise it behaves the same as the equivalent ordinary function.

In the current draft, a function is constexpr-suitable simply if it **is not a coroutine**; a non-templated constexpr function must satisfy this. All other restrictions are deferred to be checked during actual constant evaluation ([[expr.const.core]]).

A function declared with `inline` (or implicitly inline, such as a member function defined in its class, or a constexpr function). With external or module linkage it can be defined in multiple TUs, yet remains the same entity with the same address; inline substitution is only a non-binding hint.

A variable declared with `inline` (C++17), or a static data member whose first declaration has `constexpr`. Like inline functions it enjoys the ODR exemption: it can be defined in multiple TUs, and the whole program has only one object.

A template that can be used as a placeholder for a deduced class type (CTAD): a class template, a type template template parameter, or an alias template whose defining-type-id has the form `simple-template-id` (referring to another deducible template).

A deducible template name (or splice) without a template argument list, such as `std::pair` in `std::pair p(1, 2);`; it is replaced by the result of overload resolution per [[over.match.class.deduct]]. It can be used only in initializing declarations of variables (`cv T`), `new`, functional casts, and template parameters.

The value V of the constant expression `I` in `P...[I]`, which must satisfy 0 ≤ V < `sizeof...(P)`; out of range is ill-formed. The *pack-index-specifier* denotes the V-th type in the pack and is itself a pack expansion (C++26).

A placeholder type of the form `type-constraint(opt) auto` in a function parameter, lambda parameter, or template parameter; a function with one is an abbreviated function template, and a lambda with one is a generic lambda.

The process of replacing a type containing a placeholder type with the deduced type. `auto` follows the rules for template argument deduction from a function call (with `= {…}` it deduces `std::initializer_list<U>`); `decltype(auto)` follows the rules of `decltype(E)`.
